questions.prompt: Wahaj keeps a release number that people increase by hand. A teammate edits Nabd's tool schema and forgets to increase it. Which practice would have shown the change?
options: A manifest whose release id is a hash of every part
A stricter reminder in the team's release checklist
Running the evaluation set once a month
Keeping the release number in the prompt file
questions.explanation: A content hash changes whenever any part changes, whether or not anyone remembered to bump a number.
misconceptions: Relies on memory, the thing that failed
Detects a behaviour change late and does not say which part changed
Moves the number without making it follow the content

questions.prompt: Nabd's release names a provider alias that ends in "latest". What should each call's log record so that a silent model change shows up in a diff?
options: The prompt text only
The model identifier returned in the response
The alias the release asked for
The number of tokens of the answer
questions.explanation: The response names the model that actually served the call; the alias can point at a different snapshot tomorrow.
misconceptions: Assumes the prompt is the only part that can change behaviour
Records the pointer, which looks the same before and after it moves
Records a symptom that varies for many reasons

questions.prompt: Nabd's prompt, model and tools are unchanged, but the manuals index was rebuilt with a revised manual. Is this a new release?
options: No: only the data changed, not the system
No, unless the answers get worse
Yes: the index is part of what changes behaviour
Only if the index is larger than before
questions.explanation: The retrieval index decides which text the model sees, so a rebuilt index is a change to the release unit.
misconceptions: Treats the retrieval index as data outside the release
Decides by outcome after the fact instead of by what changed
Ties the release to size instead of content

questions.prompt: You retrain the champion from its registry lineage. Which evidence proves you reproduced it?
options: The same AUC on the holdout to three decimals
The same number of trees in both models
The same file name for the training data
The same data hash, the same code hash and identical predictions row by row
questions.explanation: Equal inputs (data and code hashes) and equal outputs (every prediction) are the proof; a metric alone is not.
misconceptions: Two different models can share a metric
Shape is not behaviour
A file name says nothing about its rows

questions.prompt: A retraining script reads the champion's parameters back from the tracking store and passes them straight to the trainer. It fails on the sample weight. Why?
options: The tracking store returns parameters as strings
The champion was trained with a different library
The registry deleted the parameter after promotion
Sample weights cannot be logged
questions.explanation: Parameters are stored as text, so code that retrains from the registry converts each one back to its type.
misconceptions: Guesses at the environment before reading the error
Parameters stay with the run
Confuses logging with typing

questions.prompt: A monthly batch arrives with one region's load written as a fraction. Which design stops it doing harm?
options: Train, then reject the model if its AUC falls
A contract step before training that stops the run and reports the column
A cleaning step that rescales small loads
Let the crews report odd inspection lists
questions.explanation: The contract names the broken column before any model learns from it and sends the report to the owner of the source.
misconceptions: A model trained and scored on broken data can still score well
Repairs a fault the data owner has not confirmed
Detection after the damage, by the people it hurts

questions.prompt: Why does Lab 1.3 validate the batch lazily, collecting every failure?
options: It is faster than stopping at the first failure
Because pandera cannot stop at the first failure
So the data owner can fix every problem in one delivery
So the pipeline can repair the failing rows
questions.explanation: One report with every failure saves a round trip per problem with the team that owns the export.
misconceptions: Speed is not the reason
It can; lazy is a choice
Validation reports; it does not repair

questions.prompt: A challenger beats the champion overall and is 0.07 AUC worse in one region; the gate's tolerance is 0.03. What should the gate do?
options: Promote: the overall gain outweighs one region
Raise the tolerance for this release
Promote and watch that region closely
Reject it, and record the region and the reason
questions.explanation: The regional rule is set before the release; a loss far beyond the noise in one region blocks promotion.
misconceptions: Lets an average hide the people who pay for it
Changes the rule to pass a candidate
Ships a known regression and hopes a monitor catches it

questions.prompt: Why does the promotion gate allow a small drop in a region instead of none at all?
options: A region's AUC on a few hundred feeders varies by a few hundredths between samples
Small regions matter less to the company
Challengers are always slightly worse in some region
The champion's scores are rounded
questions.explanation: Without a tolerance the gate would reject almost every challenger on sampling noise; the bootstrap measures its size.
misconceptions: Treats a fairness rule as a business weight
Not a law; it is noise
Rounding is far smaller than the tolerance

questions.prompt: Serving loads models:/fault-risk@champion. What is the release when challenger B passes the gate?
options: Copy B's model file into the service image
Move the champion alias to B, keep previous-champion on the old version, tag the reason
Delete the old champion version
Retrain B on all data and register it
questions.explanation: Moving an alias is one recorded, reversible change; the previous version stays one move away.
misconceptions: Bypasses the registry and loses the audit record
Removes the rollback
Ships a model the gate never saw

questions.prompt: Staging tested Nabd's image yesterday. Today the production job builds the image again from the same commit and deploys it. Why is this a problem?
options: The commit may have been changed since yesterday
A second build takes longer than a deploy
The production build may differ from what staging tested
Production needs a different tag than staging
questions.explanation: Only the digest that passed staging is known to work; a rebuild can pull newer base images or packages.
misconceptions: Commits are immutable; base images and packages are not
Treats the issue as speed, not identity
A different tag is still a different build

questions.prompt: Dhafer wants production deploys of Nabd to need an approval that a pull request cannot remove. Where does he put the rule on GitHub?
options: In a step of the workflow file that waits for a comment
In a branch name convention
In the README of the repository
In the production environment's protection rules
questions.explanation: Required reviewers on the environment are repository settings, outside the files a pull request can change.
misconceptions: A pull request can edit the file and remove the step
Names do not stop a job from running
Documentation does not enforce anything

questions.prompt: Dhafer merged a change to Nabd and is also on the production reviewer list. Self-review is blocked. Who can approve the release?
options: Another listed reviewer, such as Mutab
Anyone in the team with write access
Dhafer, because he is a reviewer
Nobody: the release must be merged again by someone else
questions.explanation: One approval from a listed reviewer who did not merge lets the production job start.
misconceptions: Ignores the reviewer list
Ignores the self-review rule
Invents a rule; one other reviewer is enough

questions.prompt: A candidate release of Nabd changes the prompt and the model at once, and the gate blocks it. What is the main drawback of this release?
options: It costs more to evaluate
The result does not say which change caused the block
It must be rolled back twice
The gate cannot run on two changes
questions.explanation: Changing one part per release lets a gate result point at its cause.
misconceptions: Evaluation cost is the same for any candidate
A rollback restores the whole release at once
The gate runs; the problem is reading its result

questions.prompt: A cheaper model keeps answer correctness at 0.917 but completes 5 of 6 safety procedures. The gate has a floor of 1.00 on safety steps. What is the decision?
options: Ship: the overall score is unchanged
Ship to half the crews to compare
Block, and log the safety metric and the failing case
Rerun the gate until it passes
questions.explanation: A floor with no allowed drop blocks the release on one failure; the log names the metric and the case.
misconceptions: Lets an average decide a rule written as a floor
Exposes crews to an incomplete isolation procedure
Games the gate instead of fixing the model

questions.prompt: The platform team refreshes Nabd's manuals index without changing code, prompt or model. Should the refresh go through the evaluation gate?
options: Only if the number of chunks changes
No: no code changed
No: new manuals can only improve answers
Yes: it changes what the model reads
questions.explanation: The index decides the context; a refresh is a release and is gated like one.
misconceptions: Content can change with the same chunk count
Treats code as the only part that changes behaviour
A new section can outrank the right one or split a procedure

questions.prompt: At 5% the canary served 30 requests in its pause with no problems. The analysis's minimum sample is 50. What should happen?
options: Report inconclusive and extend the pause
Roll back
Advance to 25%
Lower the minimum sample for this release
questions.explanation: Below the minimum sample there is no evidence either way: wait, then hand the decision to a person.
misconceptions: Punishes low traffic instead of a problem
Treats a quiet window as evidence
Changes the rule to fit the data

questions.prompt: Why does the canary analysis compare the candidate's graded answers with the stable version's grades on the same requests rather than with last week's average?
options: Last week's average is not stored
The same requests remove the effect of a changing question mix
It makes the canary faster
The stable version is always right
questions.explanation: The question mix changes through the day; a paired comparison leaves only the difference between versions.
misconceptions: The issue is validity, not storage
Pairing does not change speed
The stable version is a baseline, not a truth

questions.prompt: A new model snapshot passed the offline gate and 30 minutes of shadow, then failed at 25% when the next shift asked mostly in Arabic. What should change before the next attempt?
options: Skip the shadow: it was misleading
Raise the latency objective
Add Arabic cases offline and shadow across a shift change
Go straight to 50% to get a larger sample
questions.explanation: A candidate is tested only on the traffic it sees; the instruments need traffic like the failing shift.
misconceptions: Removes a safe source of evidence
Moves the rule instead of the evidence
Exposes more users to a known failure

questions.prompt: A configuration halves Mubadir's cost per model call, but its resolved share drops from 0.70 to 0.40. About how does the cost per resolved report change?
options: It halves
It is unchanged
It doubles
It falls only slightly, and unresolved reports need a person
questions.explanation: 0.5 x 0.70 / 0.40 is about 0.88 of the old cost per success, before the extra human work.
misconceptions: Divides by calls, not outcomes
Ignores both the price and the success rate
Ignores that each call is cheaper

questions.prompt: Someone added the current date as the first line of Nabd's system prompt, and the cache hit rate fell from 0.62 to 0.12. Why?
options: Prompt caches match the start of a request, and the start now changes daily
The provider stopped caching dates
Dates make prompts longer
Cached tokens expire at midnight
questions.explanation: Stable text belongs first and changing text last, so the cached prefix stays the same.
misconceptions: Invents a provider rule
Length is not the cause
The cause is the changing prefix, not expiry

questions.prompt: A month-end forecast alert fires for the fault-risk classifier on the 7th; its spend jumped on the day of the planned monthly retrain. What is the best fix?
options: Remove budget alerts for the classifier
Forecast planned jobs separately from daily running cost
Raise the classifier's budget until the alert stops
Alert only on the last day of the month
questions.explanation: A planned job inside the forecast window inflates the projection; treat it as a known item.
misconceptions: Loses the signal for real overspend
Hides the cause behind a bigger number
Too late to act

questions.prompt: Finance asks why AI costs are shown per team instead of as one platform bill. What is the main reason?
options: It is required to move money between teams
It makes the total bill smaller
Teams decide their use, so seeing their own cost changes their choices
It hides the cost of the platform team
questions.explanation: Showback puts cost in front of the people who choose how much to use.
misconceptions: That is chargeback, not showback
Showing costs does not reduce them by itself
Showback is about visibility, not hiding

questions.prompt: Nabd's logs say a request took 500 ms. What does a trace add?
options: The cost of the request
The average time of all requests that day
The text of the answer
The time of each step of that request, nested under it
questions.explanation: A trace holds one span per step with its parent and duration, so the slow step is visible.
misconceptions: Token counts can be attributes, but the point is the step breakdown
That is a metric, not a trace
Content is not what makes a trace useful, and it may hold personal data

questions.prompt: Ten traces show retrieval at 71% of request time and model calls at 27%. Where do you start?
options: Find why retrieval is slow and fix it, then measure again
Add replicas
Swap to a faster model
Remove the tool calls
questions.explanation: Fix the largest step and confirm with the same spans.
misconceptions: More copies repeat the same slow work
Optimises the smaller part
Tools are 2% of the time

questions.prompt: A developer wants to record every crew question as a span attribute. Questions sometimes contain a customer's phone number. What is the rule?
options: Record it: traces are internal
Record it only after redaction, and only if a purpose needs it
Record it only on error spans
Record it and delete the trace store yearly
questions.explanation: Data that leaves the service in traces is collected and stored; keep only what the purpose needs.
misconceptions: Traces are copied and kept by many people
Errors can contain personal data too
Stores personal data without a purpose for a year

questions.prompt: Which span name follows the OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions for one model call of Nabd?
options: nabd.model.call
LLM
chat steady
retrieval steady
questions.explanation: The conventions name a span by operation and target, such as chat with the model name.
misconceptions: A private name back ends do not recognise
Not an operation name and carries no target
Retrieval is a different operation

questions.prompt: A drift monitor alerts every hot day in summer. Which change removes these alarms but still catches a shift that lasts?
options: Raise the threshold to 2.0
Remove temperature from the monitor
Monitor once a month
Alert only on three judged days in a row
questions.explanation: Persistence filters one-day spikes and keeps sustained moves.
misconceptions: Also hides real shifts
Loses a feature that matters to the model
Delays real alerts by weeks

questions.prompt: The monitor compares each day with the previous seven days. What can it no longer see?
options: A slow drift over months
A one-day spike
A step change overnight
A day with few feeders
questions.explanation: A rolling reference absorbs slow change, so keep a fixed comparison with the training data as well.
misconceptions: It sees it; persistence decides not to alert
A step stands out against the previous week
The minimum sample handles that

questions.prompt: Serving load jumps 12% overnight while temperatures fall. The SCADA team recalibrated meters that night. What should Lamya do?
options: Retrain at once on the new values
Treat it as skew and fix the data with the SCADA team before any retraining
Ignore it: load is only one feature
Lower the alert threshold
questions.explanation: Serving computing a feature differently from training is skew; fix the data, not the model.
misconceptions: Teaches the model a measurement error
A wrong feature changes every score
The alert already worked

questions.prompt: On maintenance-freeze days only 120 feeders are scored instead of 400. Why does the monitor not judge those days?
options: The feeders are not important
The data is corrupt on those days
A small sample makes the statistic noisy
The model is not used on those days
questions.explanation: A drift statistic on a small sample moves by chance; a minimum sample avoids false alarms.
misconceptions: Importance is not the reason
The data is valid, just small
It still scores the 120

questions.prompt: Where in the online evaluation should personal data be removed from Nabd's traces?
options: Before they are shown to reviewers
Never: the grader needs it
After a year
Before they are stored
questions.explanation: Data that is never stored needs no access rule and no deletion.
misconceptions: Stored data can still be copied and read
The grader needs the answer and context, not the customer
Keeps data without purpose

questions.prompt: A grader fails 29% of sampled answers. On labelled traces it fails 90% of bad answers and passes 82% of good ones. About what failure rate do you report?
options: 15%, with the raw rate and the sample sizes
misconceptions: Reports the grader's reading as the true rate
Uses one minus sensitivity, which is not the rate
Divides by sensitivity and ignores false failures

questions.prompt: Why does the review queue include a few answers the grader passed?
options: To keep reviewers busy
To see what the grader lets through and keep its numbers current
To check the grader's speed
Because passes are usually wrong
questions.explanation: Random passes measure the grader's misses and refresh its sensitivity.
misconceptions: Not a purpose
Speed is not reviewed by people
Most passes are right

questions.prompt: Traces are kept 3 days for debugging. Some are in the review queue on day 7. What does the retention rule do with them?
options: Deletes them with the others
Keeps them forever
Holds them until reviewed, then deletes them
Keeps all traces until the queue is empty
questions.explanation: Keep data while a stated purpose needs it, then destroy it.
misconceptions: Removes data a reviewer still needs
No purpose after review
Holds unrelated data

questions.prompt: A drift alert fires on 20 September for August's feeders. August's labels are complete on 2 October. What does the retraining policy do?
options: Promote the last challenger
Retrain now on the first cut
Ignore the alert
Wait for complete labels, then retrain and gate
questions.explanation: The missing labels are the high-risk mountain feeders; training without them teaches the gap.
misconceptions: Not evidence for this change
Learns the gap where inspections are late
Discards a real signal

questions.prompt: The retraining pipeline trained a model that passed the gate. Who may promote it?
options: The model owner, recording the evidence on the version
Any engineer on call
The pipeline itself, since the gate passed
Nobody until the next quarter
questions.explanation: A person who answers for the model approves, and the approval travels with the version.
misconceptions: Not the model owner
The requester approves its own request
Delays without reason

questions.prompt: A retraining run costs 6 SAR of compute and the classifier has 26 SAR left this month. A second drift-triggered retrain is proposed. What else should the decision weigh?
options: Nothing: compute is within budget
The reviewer's time and the risk of a worse model in a region
Only the number of trees
The price of tokens
questions.explanation: Compute is the small part; review and risk are the larger costs of a retrain.
misconceptions: Ignores the review time and the risk
Not a cost
The classifier uses no tokens

questions.prompt: A drift alert on load was triaged as skew from recalibrated meters. What should the retraining trigger do?
options: Retrain early to adapt
Retrain at the next schedule with the skewed data
Not retrain; the data owner fixes the data
Lower the gate tolerance
questions.explanation: Skew is a data problem; retraining on it bakes the error into the model.
misconceptions: Learns the measurement error
Same error, later
Unrelated to the cause

questions.prompt: Which of these belongs in Mubadir's released bundle?
options: The session logs of last week
The customer database
The model provider's weights
The sandbox policy of allowed tools and readable fields
questions.explanation: Prompt, tool schemas, harness settings and sandbox policy together decide behaviour; they are versioned as one bundle.
misconceptions: Logs are produced by runs, not released
Data the agent reads is not part of its release
The bundle names a model; it does not contain it

questions.prompt: A developer adds one property to a tool schema in Mubadir's working copy. What should happen to the bundle version?
options: It changes, because a file of the bundle changed
Nothing: the prompt is unchanged
It changes only if the model is swapped
It changes at the next monthly release
questions.explanation: A content version is a hash of every file, so any change moves it.
misconceptions: Treats the prompt as the only behaviour-changing part
Ignores tools, harness and sandbox
A version follows content, not the calendar

questions.prompt: Why should Mubadir run only from the released bundle folder and record its version in each session log?
options: Because the working copy is slower
So an incident can name exactly what was running
So developers cannot read the prompt
Because session logs need a file name
questions.explanation: What ran must be what was versioned and tested; the log ties each session to it.
misconceptions: Speed is not the reason
Secrecy is not the reason
A name is not the evidence

questions.prompt: Mubadir's ticket flow crashes after creating a ticket and before notifying the crew. With a checkpointer, what does resuming the same thread do?
options: Runs the whole flow again from the start
Deletes the ticket and starts again
Runs only notify_crew, using the saved ticket id
Asks the model what to do next
questions.explanation: The checkpoint holds the state after each step, so only the missing steps run.
misconceptions: That is a restart, which opens a second ticket
Nothing is undone on resume
The saved state already says the next step

questions.prompt: The ticket service times out on create_ticket and the harness retries. Two tickets appear. What happened?
options: The model called the tool twice on purpose
The database duplicated a row
The checkpointer replayed the step
The first call committed before the timeout, so the retry wrote again
questions.explanation: A timeout does not say whether the write happened.
misconceptions: The harness retried; the model did not
Each call wrote once
Checkpoints do not run inside one step

questions.prompt: Which idempotency key makes create_ticket safe to retry?
options: A hash of the session, the tool and its arguments
A random number per call
The current time in milliseconds
The customer's account alone
questions.explanation: The key must be the same for the same intended write and different for a different one.
misconceptions: Each retry gets a new key
Each retry gets a new key
A second, different report from the same customer would be refused

questions.prompt: Which of Mubadir's tools most need an idempotency key?
options: find_customer
create_ticket and notify_crew
get_outage
None, if there is a checkpointer
questions.explanation: Writes repeat their effect on retry; reads do not.
misconceptions: A read can be retried freely
A read can be retried freely
Checkpoints do not cover a retry inside one step

questions.prompt: Why reproduce INC-0412 by replaying its recording instead of sending the same report again?
options: The customer must not be contacted again
Replay is cheaper than a model call
The recording holds the exact model outputs and tool responses
Live runs are not allowed after an incident
questions.explanation: Services and models have moved on; only the recording returns the same failure every time.
misconceptions: Not the reason the failure would hide
Cost is a side benefit, not the reason
Invents a rule

questions.prompt: In INC-0412, get_outage returned "restored" with an age of 140 minutes and Mubadir closed the report. Where does the fix belong?
options: A stronger prompt instruction only
Deleting the read replica
A larger model
A guard in the harness that blocks a close on a stale status
questions.explanation: A harness guard runs on every call and can be tested by replay.
misconceptions: Followed most of the time, not every time
Removes capacity without checking freshness
The model did what its prompt said

questions.prompt: After adding the freshness guard, which result shows that it is not simply blocking every close?
options: The case with a fresh "restored" still closes the report
The unknown-account case passes
The suite runs faster
INC-0412 now passes
questions.explanation: A regression suite keeps a case that must still succeed next to the case that must now be blocked.
misconceptions: It never reaches close_report
Speed says nothing about correctness
It would pass if every close were blocked

questions.prompt: Why put step and spend limits at the gateway and not only in the harness's max_steps?
options: The harness cannot count steps
The gateway sees every session of every version and the money spent
Gateways make calls faster
max_steps is ignored by models
questions.explanation: A bug or a new bundle can raise the harness limit; the gateway still holds.
misconceptions: It can; the gateway adds a second, shared check
Not the reason
The harness enforces it, not the model

questions.prompt: A runaway session made 80 model calls; input tokens grew from 127 to 3,609 per call. Why did it cost far more than 80 times the first call?
options: Output tokens are priced higher
The provider raised prices during the loop
Each call resends the whole conversation, so calls grow longer
Cached tokens are free
questions.explanation: Cost per call grows with the conversation, so a loop costs roughly with the square of its length.
misconceptions: Output stayed short
Invents a cause
Caching would lower the cost, not raise it

questions.prompt: Every session of Mubadir's new version loops on the same pending status. What does the kill switch stop?
options: All of Mubadir, every version
The outage service
Only the sessions that already hit the limit
That version, so the previous version or people keep serving
questions.explanation: A kill switch per version stops a shared failure without causing an outage of its own.
misconceptions: Stops the working version too
The agent is the one looping
The others would keep looping

questions.prompt: After the kill switch, what must happen to the stopped sessions?
options: Keep them with their messages and hand them to people
Restart them on the same version
Delete them to save storage
Send each customer an automatic apology
questions.explanation: Stored sessions let a person finish the work and let the incident be replayed.
misconceptions: They would loop again
Loses customers and the incident evidence
Does not finish the work

questions.prompt: In LiteLLM's proxy, which pair of settings puts a daily spend limit on a virtual key?
options: rpm_limit and tpm_limit
max_budget and budget_duration
timeout and retries
model_list and api_key
questions.explanation: max_budget with budget_duration (for example 1d) is a spend limit that resets; budgets need the proxy database.
misconceptions: Those limit rates, not spend
Those govern calls, not money
Those configure models
